text.tspan: The Mrph parameter controls the mrph output and the two phsr outputs.
When the Mrph panel control is fully counter clockwise, the mrph output will
provide the low frequency band, while the two phser outputs will provide
band pass phasers.
When the Mrph panel cotrol is fully clockwise, the mrph output will provide a
mix of the low frequency band and high frequency band, while the phsr
outputs provide six pole phasers.
As the Mrph panel control is swept across its entire range, the mrph output
will continuously crossfade from the low frequency band, to the mid
frequency band, to the high frequency band, and then to a mix of the low
frequency band and high frequency band. Simultaneously, the phsr outputs
will continuously crossfade from band pass phaser to six pole phaser,
providing a six pole all pass filter at the 12 o'clock position.
Lows + Highs
Background

text.tspan: The goal in designing the Morphing Crossover Filter (MXO) was to transform a
crossover filter into an instrument for creative sound design, while emphasizing hands
on live performance.
A combination of six pole and four pole filters seperate audio into three frequency
bands: low, mid, and high, with additional outputs for bandpass filters and phasers.
The cutoff frequency and resonance of each frequency band is adjustable both
manually and via control voltage. Resonance can be increased to self oscillation,
allowing MXO to act as a dual sine wave VCO.
A multi-channel voltage controlled crossfader allows the user to dynamically morph
between each frequency band. By modulating the cutoff frequency, resonance, and
morph control the user can achieve unique and dynamic timbre animation that would
otherwise require a rack full of modules.
MXO is 100% analog and utilizes high quality temperature compensated VCAs in its filter
cores

tspan.tspan: What is a crossover filter? :

text.tspan: A crossover filter is used to separate an audio source into distinct frequency bands.
Most often these frequency bands are routed through independent processing chains
before they are mixed back together.
An example of a basic crossover filter is a state variable filter that offers both lowpass
and highpass outputs. The lowpass and highpass outputs respectively isolate low
frequencies and high frequencies into two frequency bands.
More complex crossover filters can be made with any number of filters to separate
audio into any number of frequency bands. A lowpass filter is used to isolate low
frequencies, while a separate highpass filter is used to isolate high frequencies.
A highpass filter cascaded into a lowpass filter would then be used to isolate each mid
range band.
Consider the arrangement in the image below:
A low pass filter with a cutoff frequency of 300hz establishes the low frequency band
A high pass filter with a cutoff frequency of 300hz in series with a low pass filter with
a cutoff frequency of 4khz establishes the mid frequency band
A high pass filter with a cutoff frequency of 4khz establishes the high frequency band

tspan.tspan: Note that each frequency band shares a common cutoff frequency with its neighboring
band. This overlap allows the processed audio to be reconstructed with a flat frequency
response when the three frequency bands are mixed back together.
The cutoff frequencies specified above are arbitrary and could be adjusted as long as
neighboring frequency bands appropriately share common cutoff frequencies. For
example if the low frequency band was lowered to a cutoff frequency of 100hz, the
cutoff frequency of the highpass filter in the mid frequency band would also have to be
lowered to 100hz.
Also take note of how isolating low frequencies and high frequencies only requires one
filter each, but isolating the mid frequency band requires two filters. A mid frequency
band therefore has two points of adjustment, the cutoff frequency for the high pass filter
and the cutoff frequency for the low pass filter. The distance between these two cutoff
frequencies determines the bandwidth of the mid frequency band. A wide bandwidth
corresponds to more frequencies within that frequency band, while a narrow bandwidth
corresponds to less frequencies within that frequency band. Keep this in mind when we
discuss the spread parameter later in the manual.
Take a look at the following image and note how the bandwidth of the mid frequency
band has been expanded and that the low and high frequency bands have been
adjusted accordingly.

text.tspan: A common application of a crossover filter is a multiband compressor: Incoming audio is
separated into several frequency bands, which are then routed through their own
individual compressors before they are mixed back together. This allows the mix engineer
to have independent control of the dynamics for different frequency ranges. For example,
you could heavily compress the mid range, while leaving the lows and highs more open.
While MXO offers individual outputs per frequency band, the primary focus of the
instrument is not to individually process each band and then mix them back together.
Rather the focus is to use the three frequency bands to create three distinct timbral
variations of the input and then use the morph control to dynamically crossfade between
each timbral variation. This results in timbral modulation that creates a unique sense of
movement and texture in your patches.
Installation
MXO has a width of 24hp and a depth of 38.1mm (1.5 inches). MXO draws 190ma from
both the +12V and -12V power rails and is reverse power protected.
Before placing MXO in your rack, turn off the power to your Eurorack case and then
properly install the power ribbon cable on both the module and your case's PSU bus
board. MXO comes with a keyed power header, the key on the ribbon cable must align
with the notch on the power header. The red line on the ribbon cable must align with the
-12V label printed on the module and on your case’s PSU busboard.
If you cannot align both the key/notch and the redline/-12V label, find a new ribbon
cable. After double checking the ribbon cable, place the module in your case and secure
it with the screws of your choosing.
Start Up Procedure
When you first power on your rack, MXO runs through an internal analog startup procedure.
This ensures that the circuit starts up in a stable state. Please allow about 10 seconds for the
startup procedure to finish. The module is ready to be used when the LED lights up.
Architecture
The foundation of MXO is a voltage controlled six pole state variable filter, a unique filter
topology that has never been offered in a commercial synthesizer. The six pole state
variable filter simultaneously provides a low pass filter, high pass filter, band pass filter,
and a unique band pass phaser, all with 36 dB/oct slopes. Pole mixing is then used to
provide a six pole phaser and six pole all pass filter.
Two six pole state variable filters along with a four pole state variable filter separate
incoming audio into low, mid, and high frequency bands:
The low frequency band is defined as a six pole low pass filter.
The mid frequency band is defined as a four pole high pass filter and a six pole low
pass filter in series.
The high frequency band is defined as a six pole high pass filter in series with a non-
resonant two pole low pass filter.
The additional two pole low pass filter allows the user to attenuate high frequencies to
taste. This is especially useful when monitoring the morph output because it can prevent
sudden harsh timbre transitions when crossfading into the high frequency band.
The band pass and phaser outputs greatly expand MXO's capabilities well past that of a
standard crossover filter. The band pass filters, with their steep slopes, are great for
formant effects, while the two phaser outputs are perfect for lush stereo sounds with lots
of movement.
The block diagram below ilustrates MXO's signal flow and how the filters work together
to achieve the wide range of functionality. Each block represents a function, namely a
filter, crossfader, or VCA. The left side of each block is the function's input, while the right
side is the function's output(s). The top or bottom of each block shows the function's

text.tspan: Standards
All parameters on shkrjn-instruments modules are designed to respond to a range of 10V.
Think of it this way: a knob that is fully counter clockwise corresponds to 0V and a knob
that is fully clockwise corresponds to 10V. A knob positioned at 12 o’clock corresponds to
0V
5V
When a knob is marked with “O” directly above it, the 12 o’clock position corresponds to
0V. Thus the fully counter clockwise position corresponds to -5V, while the fully clockwise
position corresponds to 5V. The entire range of the knob is still 10V.
0V
5V
The same concept applies to attenuators. When an attenuator for a CV input is marked
with “O” directly above it, that indicates a bipolar attenuator, sometimes called an
attenuverter. This means that the 12 o’clock position corresponds to no modulation, while
the fully counter clockwise position corresponds to 100% inverted modulation and the
fully clockwise position corresponds to 100% non inverted modulation.
When an attenuator is not accompanied by “O”, that indicates a standard unipolar
attenuator. The fully counter clockwise position corresponds to no modulation, while the
fully clockwise position corresponds to 100% modulation.
Imagine that a parameter's panel control is positioned at 12 o’clock and the parameter is
being modulated by a bipolar LFO with a range of +/- 5V. This has the same effect as
sweeping that knob across its entire range from fully counter-clockwise to fully clockwise:
Imagine that the same panel control is positioned fully counter clockwise and the
associated parameter is modulated by a unipolar envelope with an amplitude of 10V. This
also has the same effect as sweeping that knob across its entire range from counter
clockwise to clockwise.
This is the behavior that is being described when you encounter the following text: “CV
applied to the X input sums with the X knob position after it passes through the bipolar
attenuator. The expected range of this sum is 10V.”
The Freq parameter controls the cutoff frequencies of all of the filters
simultaneously. Turning the Freq panel control clockwise will increase all
cutoff frequencies, while turning it counter clockwise will decrease all
cutoff frequencies. The cutoff frequency range is 20hz - 20khz.
CV applied to the FM input modulates the Freq parameter. The FM input’s
associated bipolar attenuator determines the amplitude and polarity of the
CV applied to the FM input. CV applied to the FM input sums with the
Freq knob position after it passes through the bipolar attenuator. The
expected range of this sum is 10V.

text.tspan: The Spread parameter is used to spread apart the low and
high frequency bands, while simultaneously expanding the
bandwidth of the mid frequency band.
When the spread panel control is fully counter clockwise the
cutoff frequencies for all filters are equal.
As the spread panel control is turned clockwise, the cutoff frequency for
the low frequency band decreases while the cutoff frequency for the high
frequency band increases.
As a result, the bandwidth of the mid frequency band expands, always
filling the space between the low and high frequency bands.
Neighboring frequency bands always share common cutoff frequencies as
laid out in the background section, which allows smooth transitioning
between frequency bands when using the morph control.
CV applied to the spread input modulates the spread parameter.
The associated bipolar attenuator determines the amplitude and polarity
of the CV applied to the spread input. After the CV passes through the
bipolar attenuator, it sums with the spread knob position. The expected
range of this sum is 10V.
v/oct 1
v/oct 2

text.tspan: The animations below illustrate the effect of increasing the spread control.
Notice that when the low and high frequency bands overlap, the mid frequency band
is attenuated and has an excessively narrow bandwidth.
Low Freq CV
High Freq CV
Low Freq CV
Damp CV
Low Freq CV = Freq + FM + v/Oct 1 - Spread
Morph CV
Morph CV
Morph CV
High Freq CV = Freq + FM + v/Oct 2 + Spread
Two volt per octave inputs allow the cutoff frequencies of the filters to
follow pitch sequences, which is especially useful when MXO is being
used as a dual oscillator.
v/Oct 1 affects the low frequency band, bp 1, phsr 1, and the high pass
filter of the mid frequency band.
v/Oct 2 affects the high frequency band, bp 2, phsr 2, and the low pass
filter of the mid frequency band.
When nothing is patched to v/Oct 2, it responds to the voltage present at v/Oct 1.
The relationship between the v/Oct inputs and the various filters is more intuitive when
you look at the signal flow block diagram and take note of how MXO's various outputs
correspond to the different filter blocks.
The band pass filters and phasers are affected by spread in a similar fashion. As spread
increases the two band pass filters and phasers diverge from one another across the
frequency spectrum. When spread is fully counter clockwise, the cutoff frequency of
the two band pass filters and phasers are equal.
VCA
VCA CV

tspan.tspan: Resonance Control:

text.tspan: res
The Res parameter controls the resonance of all of the filters simultaneously.
When the Res panel control is fully counter clockwise the filters are non
resonant and have a butterworth response. Resonance can be increased all
the way to self oscillation, the onset of which is slow and begins around the 3
o'clock position.
CV applied to the Res input modulates the Res parameter. The Res input’s
associated bipolar attenuator determines the amplitude and polarity of the
CV applied to the Res input. CV applied to the Res input sums with the Res
panel control after it passes through the bipolar attenuator. The expected
range of this sum is 10V.
Because the mid frequency band is made up of two filters in series, when the
spread parameter is fully counter clockwise, moderate to high resonance
settings can cause extreme clipping. The reason for this is that when the two
filters have equal cutoff frequencies, the resonance of the second filter
amplifies the resonance of the first filter. To prevent unwanted clipping
attenuate the input, increase the spread amount, or utilize Tilt to rely on one
filter for resonance.

text.tspan: The Tilt parameter is used to increase the resonance of one set of filters,
while decreasing the resonance of the other set of filters.
When the Tilt panel control is positioned at 12 o'clock, all filters are
equally resonant. As Tilt is turned clockwise, the resonance of the high
frequency band increases along with the resonance of the mid frequency
band's low pass filter. Simultaneously, the resonance of the low freqency
band decreases along with the resonance of the mid frequency band's
high pass filter.
As Tilt is turned counter clockwise from its center position, the resonance
of the low frequency band increases along with the mid frequency band's
high pass filter. Simultaneously, the resonance of the high frequency band
decreases along with the resonance of the mid frequency band's low pass
filter.
The band pass filters and phasers are affected in a similar fashion. As Tilt
is turned clockwise the resonance of BP 2 and Phsr 2 increases, while the
resonance of BP 1 and Phsr 1 decreases.
When Tilt is turned counter clockwise the resonance of BP 1 and Phsr 1
increases, while the resonance of BP 2 and Phsr 2 decreases.
The Tilt parameter is weighted such that when the Res panel control is at 12 o'clock,
turning Tilt fully clockwise or counter clockwise will cause one set of filters to oscillate,
while causing the other set of filters to be minimally resonant.
CV applied to the Tilt input modulates the Tilt parameter. The associated bipolar
attenuator determines the amplitude and polarity of this modulation. CV applied to the
Tilt input sums with Tilt panel control after it passes through the bipolar attenuator. The
expected range of this sum is 10V.
The animations below demonstrate sweeping the Res and Tilt panel controls across
their entire range. The first animation demonstrates Res and the second illustrates Tilt.
For the Tilt animation, assume that the Res panel control is positioned at 12 o'clock
and that the Tilt panel control is first turned clockwise from 12 o'clock and then counter
clockwise from 12 o'clock.
While these animations demonstrate the functionality of Res and Tilt, the real life
amplitude response of MXO's resonance may differ slightly.
trk
damp
The Damp control determines the cut off frequency of the Damp filter,
which is a non resonant two pole low pass filter applied to the high
frequency band. The purpose of the damp filter is to tame the high
frequencies of the high frequency band to prevent sudden and harsh
timbre transitions when monitoring the morph output. If you do not
wish to attenuate the high frequencies, turn the damp control fully
clockwise. Its range exceeds 20khz to minimze unwanted attenuation.
The "trk" switch engages or disengages tracking. When tracking is engaged, the damp
filter follows the cutoff frequency of the high frequency band's six pole high pass filter.
The damp panel control then acts as a frequency offset. This is useful for programming a
fixed bandwidth that stays consistent as the high frequency band travels across the
frequency spectrum.
When tracking is disengaged, the damp filter's cutoff frequency is completely
independent and only responds to the damp panel control and its associated CV input.
This is useful for subtle high frequency attenuation that stays consistent despite the
movement of the high frequency band's six pole high pass filter. This also allows the
damp filter's cut off frequency to be lower than the cut off frequency of the high
frequncy band's six pole high pass filter, which can result in full attenuation of the high
frequency band.
Tracking is engaged when the "trk" switch is positioned upwards.
Tracking is disengaged when the "trk" switch is positioned downwards.
The damp control can be modulated via the aux input when the associated switch is set
to "damp". There is no attenuator for this CV input. The CV sums with the Damp panel
control and the expected range of this sum is 10V.

When tracking is disengaged, start with the damp panel control
fully clockwise and then turn it counter clockwise to determine
how much high frequency content you wish to attenuate.
When tracking is engaged, start with the damp panel control fully counter clockwise
and then turn it clockwise to determine the bandwidth of the high frequency band.

tspan.tspan: Morph Control:

text.tspan: The lines on the Mrph dial mark the positions to target the different frequency bands
and phaser modes
mrph
mrph
Lows
Mids
Highs
Lows + Highs
BP Phaser
Phaser
All Pass Filter
CV applied to the mrph input modulates the Mrph parameter. The associated bipolar
attenuator determines the amplitude and polarity of this modulation. The CV applied
to the mrph input sums with the panel control after it passes through the bipolar
attenuator. The expected range of this sum is 10V.
The two animations below demonstrate the frequency response of the mrph output
and two phsr outputs as the mrph panel control is swept from its fully counter clockwise
position to its fully clockwise position. Note that in reality the morphing behavior is
continuous rather than stepped. Also note that while the phaser animations accurately
demonstrate the phaser's frequency responses, the nuances of their responses may
differ IRL.

text.tspan: The amplitude of the mrph output can be modulated via an internal VCA.
To modulate the VCA, apply CV to the AUX input and position the associated switch to the
right.
There is no attenuator or panel control for the VCA's CV. When nothing is patched to
the AUX input or when the AUX input's switch is positioned to the left, the VCA will
automitcally be held open by an internal CV.
The VCA CV input only responds to positive voltage and expects a range of 8V to
accomdate envelopes that adhere to the Doepfer standard. Voltages outside of the 0 -
8V range will not damage the module as long as they do not exceed +/- 12V.

text.tspan: "In" marks the main audio input for MXO. This input is accompanied by
an attenuator, which has an attenuation range of about 20dB. The
character of MXO's resonance varies depending on the amplitude of the
incoming audio signal. The limited range of the input attenuator allows
the user to fine tune how the resonance responds to incoming audio.
The animations below demonstrate two uses of the damp filter. In the first animation
tracking is disengaged, which allows the damp filter and the high frequency band's six
pole high pass filter to be adjusted independently. Note that when the cutoff frequency
of the damp filter is lower than the cutoff frequency of the six pole high pass filter, the
high frequency band fades into silence.
In the second animation tracking is engaged. The cut off frequency of the six pole high
pass filter is adjusted, causing the damp filter to adjust in unison. This allows the high
frequency band to maintain a fixed bandwidth as it travels along the frequency
spectrum. Note that when tracking is engaged, the Damp filter's cutoff frequency
cannot be lower than the cutoff frequency of the high frequency band's high pass filter.
